summary: Defines extensions to BGP-4 so it can carry routing information for several network layer protocols, such as IPv6. The extensions are backward compatible, so routers with and without them can still work together. It was replaced by RFC 2858.

eli5.summary: One routing system learns to carry directions for more than one kind of address, without confusing routers that only know the old kind.

questions: how are bgp attributes backward compatible
subtitle: Routing protocol extensions for multiple address families.

tldr.problem: BGP-4 was designed to exchange routing information only for IPv4 addresses, but networks also need to route other protocols like IPv6 and IPX.
tldr.mechanism: Extensions add two new optional attributes (MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI) that let routers advertise reachable and unreachable routes for any network layer protocol identified by an Address Family number.
tldr.outcome: BGP-4 routers can now exchange routes for multiple protocols while remaining compatible with unmodified BGP-4 routers that simply ignore the new attributes.

today: RFC 2283 was a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 2858, which provides a revised multiprotocol specification.

sections.title: The Limitation
sections.content:
BGP-4 (Border Gateway Protocol version 4, defined in RFC 1771) is the routing protocol the Internet uses to exchange reachability information between autonomous systems. However, it was designed exclusively for IPv4: the original 32-bit Internet address format.

As IPv6 and other protocols emerged, BGP-4 routers could not advertise routes for them. A router had no way to tell its peers "I can reach this IPv6 address" or "I can reach this IPX network." The protocol needed to grow without breaking existing deployments.
sections.eli5: BGP is how routers tell each other where to find IP addresses. But it only knew IPv4 addresses. When IPv6 and other protocols arrived, it was stuck.

sections.title: The Multiprotocol Approach
sections.content:
The RFC identifies exactly three pieces of BGP-4 that are IPv4-specific: the NEXT_HOP attribute (which holds the IPv4 address of the next router), the AGGREGATOR attribute (which also contains IPv4 addresses), and NLRI (Network Layer Reachability Information, which lists the IPv4 address prefixes being advertised). To support multiple network layer protocols, BGP-4 needs only two additions:

  • A way to associate a network layer protocol with the next hop information.
  • A way to associate a network layer protocol with NLRI.

Each protocol is identified using an Address Family Identifier (from RFC 1700). To maintain backward compatibility, the new information is carried in optional, non-transitive attributes. A router that does not understand multiprotocol extensions simply ignores these new attributes and passes them along unchanged.
sections.eli5: Routers only need to learn two new skills: remembering what kind of address a route is for (IPv4 vs. IPv6) and how to say "I don't know this new thing" without breaking.

sections.title: The New Attributes
sections.content:
Two new optional, non-transitive attributes carry multiprotocol information:

MP_REACH_NLRI (Type Code 14) advertises reachable routes for a particular network layer protocol. It contains a 2-octet Address Family Identifier, a 1-octet Subsequent Address Family Identifier (providing additional detail such as whether the routes are for unicast, multicast, or both), the network address of the next hop, optional subnetwork attachment information (SNPAs), and the network layer reachability information for destinations reachable via that next hop.

MP_UNREACH_NLRI (Type Code 15) withdraws (removes from service) routes for a particular protocol. It contains the Address Family Identifier, the Subsequent Address Family Identifier, and the withdrawn routes. Unlike MP_REACH_NLRI, it requires no next hop information because withdrawn routes need only be removed.

Because these attributes are optional and non-transitive, a BGP speaker that receives an UPDATE message carrying them but does not understand them simply ignores them and does not forward them to other peers.
sections.eli5: The two new message types are labeled with what kind of address they are for, just like a mailbox is labeled with a house number and street.

sections.title: Interoperability and Rules
sections.content:
Routers using multiprotocol extensions follow strict rules to ensure correct operation. For example, a BGP speaker must never advertise its own address as the next hop for a route it originates, and must never install a route with itself as the next hop. When advertising a route to an external peer, the next hop can be the router's own interface (a "first party" next hop), an internal peer's interface (a "third party" next hop), or an external peer's interface (another form of third party next hop).

Any UPDATE message carrying MP_REACH_NLRI must also carry the ORIGIN and AS_PATH attributes, and in internal BGP (IBGP) exchanges must also include LOCAL_PREF. If such a message comes from an external peer, the router checks that the leftmost AS in the AS_PATH matches the peer's autonomous system number; if not, it sends a NOTIFICATION message with an error.
sections.eli5: When routers talk to each other about routes, they follow traffic rules so nobody gets confused about where packets should go.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The design ensures that multiprotocol-enabled routers can coexist with standard BGP-4 routers. A router that does not support the multiprotocol extensions will ignore MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI attributes in received UPDATE messages, because they are marked optional and non-transitive. The router continues to function normally, processing only the standard IPv4 NLRI and next hop information.

This one-way compatibility means a deployment can gradually introduce multiprotocol support. New routers can advertise IPv6 routes to each other while still exchanging IPv4 routes with legacy routers. The RFC reserves values 128-255 in the Subsequent Address Family Identifier field for vendor-specific uses, and requires IETF consensus and IESG approval for assigning other new values.
sections.eli5: Old routers simply skip the new multiprotocol labels and keep working, so you can upgrade some routers without breaking the old ones.
